articles.title: Musk throws $276M behind Republicans in midterms
articles.summary: Tech trillionaire Elon Musk gave $276 million to several Republican super PACs and organizations over the past three months, as the GOP faces headwinds ahead of the midterm elections. This brings the Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s total contributions so far to $366 million. A spokesperson for Musk’s America PAC confirmed the numbers to The Hill,…
articles.body:
Tech trillionaire Elon Musk gave $276 million to several Republican super PACs and organizations over the past three months, as the GOP faces headwinds ahead of the midterm elections .

This brings the Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s total contributions so far to $366 million. A spokesperson for Musk’s America PAC confirmed the numbers to The Hill, which were first reported by The New York Times.

Between July and September, Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, and $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which supports GOP House candidates.

The move signals Musk’s appetite for political involvement, despite his suggestions he could pull back spending for the midterms.

Musk’s America PAC, which he launched during the 2024 election, received more than $76 million. He also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC backing Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, said in a statement to the Times and confirmed by The Hill.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo added.

The Hill reached out to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the Republican Governors Association, the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Lone Star Liberty PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund for comment.

Musk’s latest donations make him the largest known donor in the 2026 midterms, the Times reported. Musk, who long stayed out of politics, jumped into the political world during the 2024 elections, pouring hundreds of millions into the presidential race for Trump.

He joined the then-candidate on the campaign trail and later led Trump’s cost-cutting effort known as the Department of Government Efficiency. The project sparked controversy for its sweeping job and funding cuts across the federal government.

He departed the White House in late May 2025 and, after a public fallout with Trump, stayed quiet for months in the political space. Musk said last May he planned to spend “a lot less” on politics, and he later told The Economist in a July interview he “got carried away” and “a little too involved in politics.”

Still, the world’s richest person jumped back into the political fray that same month, authorizing America PAC to spend $100 million to $120 million for a new field program focused on conservative voter turnout in the 2026 midterms.

Musk and Trump have since rekindled their alliance following the blowout, and the tech billionaire joined the president for his state visit to China in May, along with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month.

articles.title: Pentagon data breach exposes records of over 3M people
articles.summary: The Pentagon data breach exposed 2.76 million Social Security numbers and military records, raising long-term identity theft concerns for veterans.
articles.body: You can change a password after a breach. You can cancel a credit card. But when your Social Security number gets exposed, you could be dealing with the fallout for years. That is the concern after a major breach involving the Pentagon's Defense Manpower Data Center. If you have served in the military, worked for the Department of War or have other ties to the military community, your information could be among the records involved. A War Department official told CyberGuy that 2.76 million living individuals and 294,000 deceased individuals were affected. Depending on the person, the exposed information can include Social Security numbers, names, dates of birth, contact information and military personnel details. So, if a breach letter from the Pentagon shows up in your mailbox, don't toss it aside. Here's what happened, what may have been exposed and what you can do to protect yourself. DMV BREACH CONFIRMED AS HACKERS CLAIM 200,000 RECORDS STOLEN Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com How the Pentagon data breach happened The breach involved the Defense Manpower Data Center, or DMDC. A War Department official told CyberGuy that a DMDC information system experienced unauthorized access to personally identifiable information by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. The official said DMDC immediately remediated the vulnerability after discovering it. At this time, the department says it has no indication that the accessed information has been misused. The files accessed contained unencrypted personally identifiable information. That created a potentially long exposure window before the vulnerability was discovered. Personal information such as a Social Security number can remain useful to criminals long after the original breach fades from the headlines. What information was exposed in the Pentagon breach The specific information varies depending on the person. According to the Pentagon, exposed records can include: The military details make this breach particularly sensitive because the records may reveal more than basic identity information. DMDC plays a major role behind the scenes at the Department of Defense. It maintains more than 60 million records covering military personnel, civilian employees, contractors, family members, retirees and veterans. The agency uses those records to support benefits, identity verification and other Defense Department programs. In other words, plenty of people who left active military service years ago may still have information stored in these systems. How to know if the Pentagon breach affected you People whose personal information was accessed are being notified by postal mail through the Department's contracted provider, Identity Theft Guard Solutions, or IDX. If you receive a notice, read it carefully rather than assuming it is another piece of junk mail. The letter should explain what information tied to you was affected and what protection is being offered. According to the War Department official, IDX is providing notification, credit monitoring and identity restoration support based on the data elements affected for each individual. Anyone with questions can visit response.idx.us/DMDC or call 1-855-744-4556. Be careful with unexpected emails or text messages claiming to be connected to the breach. Scammers can use major security incidents as an excuse to send fake notices or links designed to steal even more information. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected message, verify the information using the official IDX contact details or the postal notice you received. WHY SCAMMERS TARGET VETERANS AND HOW TO FIGHT BACK Why stolen Social Security numbers create a long-term risk A credit card number has an expiration date. Your Social Security number usually stays with you for life. That can give criminals plenty of time to combine stolen information from one breach with information collected elsewhere. Someone might already have your phone number or an old email address. Adding a Social Security number and date of birth can make a stolen identity far more useful. A criminal could try to open credit in your name or use the information in a convincing phishing attack. Other forms of identity fraud may never involve your credit report at all. That is why I would treat a breach involving an SSN differently from one exposing an email address or password. What to do if your information was exposed A breach notice can leave you wondering where to start, so focus first on the protections that can limit what someone does with the information. 1) Enroll in the free monitoring if you are eligible If DMDC sent you an official notification, review the identity protection services available to you. Eligible individuals may receive 12 months of free credit monitoring and identity restoration support through IDX, depending on the information affected. Credit monitoring can warn you about certain changes to your credit file. However, monitoring usually alerts you after activity occurs. It does not stop someone from attempting to use your identity. If you were not contacted by DMDC, or if you want protection that continues beyond the free 12-month period, you may also want to consider a broader identity theft protection service. Depending on the service, it may monitor for suspicious use of your personal information and provide help if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 2) Freeze your credit Consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze restricts access to your credit file, which can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name. You can temporarily lift the freeze when you legitimately need to apply for credit. A freeze remains one of the strongest free steps you can take after your Social Security number has been exposed. Keep in mind that a freeze focuses on new credit. It cannot stop every type of identity theft, including fraud involving an existing account. 3) Consider placing a fraud alert If you do not want to freeze your credit, you can place a fraud alert on your credit reports. A fraud alert tells lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening new credit. You only need to contact one of the three major credit bureaus, and that bureau should notify the other two. A fraud alert offers less protection than a freeze, but it can still add another layer of scrutiny. PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBERS, PERSONAL INFO OF 2.76M US MILITARY, CIVILIAN PERSONNEL 4) Watch your existing accounts Review your bank and credit card activity regularly. Also pay attention to unexpected changes involving accounts that use your identity. Turn on transaction alerts where available. Quick warnings can help you spot activity before it grows into a bigger problem. 5) Be suspicious of messages about the breach and use strong antivirus software Scammers pay attention to major data breaches too. You could receive a call, email or text from someone claiming to represent the Defense Department, a credit monitoring company or another organization offering to help you secure your identity. Do not hand over a Social Security number, password or verification code because someone contacts you unexpectedly. Also avoid opening attachments or clicking links in unexpected breach-related messages. Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious links and other threats that may show up in follow-up scams. Keep your security software updated and verify unexpected requests using official contact information you find yourself. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 6) Protect important accounts with two-factor authentication Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services whenever it is available. Your email account deserves special attention because criminals can use it to reset passwords for other accounts. An authenticator app or passkey can offer stronger protection than relying only on a password. 7) Get an IRS Identity Protection PIN If your Social Security number was exposed, consider getting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. An IP PIN is a six-digit number that helps prevent someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new PIN each year. This can be especially useful after a breach because tax-related identity theft may not show up on a credit report. 8) Keep watching after the free monitoring ends One year of free monitoring is useful, but stolen personal information does not become harmless when that year expires. Continue checking your credit reports and financial accounts. Also pay attention to unexpected tax notices, benefit claims or bills that you do not recognize. We have previously explained why a credit freeze alone does not stop every form of identity theft. A stolen Social Security number can potentially be misused in ways that never trigger a traditional credit check. Kurt's key takeaways What stands out to me here is how long the information involved can remain valuable. A password can be replaced in a few minutes, but a Social Security number, birth date or military history can follow you for decades. If you receive one of these Pentagon breach notices, I would take it seriously even though officials say they have not seen evidence of misuse. Use the free monitoring being offered and consider freezing your credit. Then keep an eye on your accounts after that free monitoring period ends. We hand organizations an enormous amount of personal information because we often have no practical alternative. When that information gets exposed, the burden of watching for fraud suddenly falls back on us. If the government loses information as sensitive as your Social Security number, should it be responsible for protecting your identity for longer than one year? articles.title: Tropical tracker: Timeline of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season
articles.summary: Each year, the Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through Nov. 30. Follow along as we track each storm throughout the season.
articles.body:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — Each year, the Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 through Nov. 30. This year is expected to have fewer storms than usual, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicting a below-average season .

Follow along as we track each storm throughout hurricane season. Looking for a previous year? Here are our timelines for 2024 and 2025 .

There are no active storms at this time.

June 16, 10 a.m.: The National Hurricane Center identified Potential Tropical Cyclone One about 65 miles southwest of Corpus Christi, Texas. PTC One had maximum sustained winds of 30 mph and was moving northeast at 6 mph.

June 16, 4 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Louisiana coast from Sabine Pass to Morgan City.

June 17, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Arthur formed about 40 miles east-northeast of Port O’Connor, Texas. Arthur had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was moving northeast at 9 mph. A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Texas coast from High Island to the Louisiana border.

June 17, 11:30 a.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Texas coast from Sargent to High Island.

June 17, 10 p.m.: Tropical Storm Arthur became a post-tropical cyclone about 35 miles north-northeast of Galveston, Texas. Arthur had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving northeast at 9 mph.

July 19, 10 a.m.: Tropical Depression Two formed about 155 miles south of Panama City, Florida. TD Two had maximum sustained winds of 30 mph and was moving north-northwest at 2 mph.

July 20, 7 p.m.: Tropical Depression Two strengthened into Tropical Storm Bertha about 110 miles south of Panama City, Florida. Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was moving west-northwest at 3 mph.

July 20, 10 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Gulf Coast between the Alabama-Florida border and the Jefferson-Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana.

July 21, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Bertha reached its maximum strength , with 60 mph winds. A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Florida coast from the Alabama border to the Bay-Gulf line border, and for the Louisiana coast from the Jefferson-Plaquemines parish line to the Terrebonne-Lafourche parish line.

July 21, 4 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Louisiana coast from the Terrebonne-Lafourche parish line to Morgan City, and for Metropolitan New Orleans and Lake Ponchartrain.

July 22, 2 p.m.: Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall near the Biloxi Wildlife Management Area in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana. Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph and was moving west-northwest at 7 mph.

July 22, 4 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Louisiana coast from Morgan City to Cameron.

July 22, 10 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued between Cameron, Louisiana, and Sargent, Texas.

July 23, 1 p.m.: Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border. Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph and was moving west at 10 mph.

July 23, 7 p.m.: Tropical Storm Bertha weakened to a tropical depression about 10 miles north-northeast of Houston, Texas. Bertha had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving west at 13 mph.

July 23, 10 p.m. : Tropical Depression Bertha dissipated about 40 miles west-northwest of Houston, Texas.

Aug. 12, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Cristobal formed about 880 miles west of the Azores. Cristobal had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph and was moving east at 25 mph.

Aug. 13, 4 a.m.: Tropical Storm Cristobal weakened to a tropical depression about 610 miles west of the Azores. Cristobal had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving northeast at 16 mph.

Aug. 13, 10 a.m.: Tropical Depression Cristobal became a post-tropical remnant low about 535 miles west-northwest of the Azores. Cristobal had maximum sustained winds of 30 mph and was moving northeast at 16 mph.

Aug. 27, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Dolly formed about 1,555 miles east of the Leeward Islands. Dolly had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was moving west at 24 mph.

Aug. 28, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Dolly dissipated about 1,000 miles east of the Leeward Islands.

Aug. 31, 10 a.m.: The National Hurricane Center identified Potential Tropical Cyclone Five about 130 miles south of Morgan City, Louisiana. PTC Five had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving west-northwest at 5 mph. A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Gulf coast between Port Bolivar, Texas, and the Vermilion-Cameron parish line in Louisiana.

Aug. 31, 1 p.m.: Tropical Depression Five formed about 120 miles south-southeast of Morgan City, Louisiana. TD Five had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving west-northwest at 5 mph.

Aug. 31, 4 p.m.: A Tropical Storm Warning was issued for the Louisiana coast from the Vermilion-Cameron parish line to the Vermilion-Iberia parish line.

Aug. 31, 7 p.m.: Tropical Depression Five strengthened into Tropical Storm Edouard about 140 miles southeast of Cameron, Louisiana. Edouard had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was moving west-northwest at 6 mph.

Sept. 1, 2 p.m.: Tropical Storm Edouard reached its maximum strength , with 60 mph winds.

Sept. 1, 2:20 p.m.: Tropical Storm Edouard made landfall near Johnson Bayou, Louisiana. Edouard had maximum sustained winds of 60 mph and was moving northwest at 8 mph.

Sept. 1, 10 p.m.: Tropical Storm Edouard weakened to a tropical depression about 40 miles northwest of Beaumont, Texas. Edouard had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving northwest at 8 mph.

Sept. 3, 4 a.m.: Tropical Depression Edouard dissipated about 40 miles southeast of Dallas, Texas.

Sept. 19, 10 a.m.: Tropical Depression Six formed about 525 miles southwest of the Azores. TD Six had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving north at 2 mph.

Sept. 20, 4 a.m.: Tropical Depression Six strengthened into Tropical Storm Fay about 450 miles southwest of the Azores. Fay had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph and was moving north-northeast 5 mph.

Sept. 20, 10 p.m.: Tropical Storm Fay reached its maximum strength , with 70 mph winds.

Sept. 22, 10 a.m.: Tropical Storm Fay weakened to a tropical depression about 645 miles southwest of the Azores. Fay had maximum sustained winds of 35 mph and was moving southwest at 10 mph.

Sept. 22, 4 p.m.: Tropical Depression Fay dissipated about 685 miles southwest of the Azores.

articles.title: Flood damaged EVs pose fire risk even after water recedes, fire officials say
articles.summary: Saltwater can damage lithium-ion batteries found in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters, potentially triggering fires days or even weeks after the initial exposure.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Following coastal flooding in Southern California this week, fire officials are warning residents about a potentially dangerous consequence of saltwater exposure involving electric vehicles and other battery-powered transportation.

The Laguna Beach Fire Department said saltwater can damage lithium-ion batteries found in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters, potentially triggering fires days or even weeks after the initial exposure.

Flash flood warnings have been issued for portions of Orange, Riverside and Imperial counties as a result of post-Tropical Storm Rachel moving through the region and bringing widespread coastal flooding.

The storm has already battered coastal communities, including Long Beach, Newport Beach and Malibu, where powerful waves and unusually high tides have flooded streets, damaged infrastructure and prompted emergency measures.

In Long Beach, mandatory evacuations were ordered for homes along portions of Seaside Walk after several structures were deemed unsafe to occupy.

Along the Los Angeles County coastline, a coastal flood warning remained in effect until 3 p.m. Sunday, with forecasters warning that high tides approaching 8 feet and surf of 5 to 8 feet could produce significant flooding and beach erosion.

Officials warned that even vehicles that appear to be operating normally could pose a fire risk if floodwater reached their batteries or electrical components.

Residents who suspect their vehicle sustained saltwater damage, including those whose vehicles were partially submerged, are urged not to drive or charge them.

Instead, fire officials recommend contacting their insurance company, arranging for professional towing and having the vehicle inspected by a certified mechanic qualified to service electric or hybrid vehicles.

The warning also applies to e-bikes and electric scooters that may have been exposed to coastal floodwaters.

According to the department, warning signs of a potentially dangerous battery include smoke, hissing or popping sounds and unusual heat.

Anyone noticing those signs should immediately move away from the vehicle and call 911.

Officials cautioned residents against attempting to move a vehicle exhibiting those warning signs or trying to extinguish a battery fire themselves.

The department emphasized that the danger may not be immediately apparent, with battery fires potentially occurring long after floodwaters have receded.

KTLA Digital Producer Lily Dallow contributed to this report.

articles.summary: Delta Air Lines said Monday it will postpone the launch of its flight service from Atlanta to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched deadly attacks on the latter city’s King Khalid International Airport. Citing “evolving developments in the region,” Delta said in a release it was delaying the launch until March. The…
articles.body:
Delta Air Lines said Monday it will postpone the launch of its flight service from Atlanta to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched deadly attacks on the latter city’s King Khalid International Airport.

Citing “evolving developments in the region,” Delta said in a release it was delaying the launch until March. The nonstop flight service from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport to Riyadh was scheduled to start on Oct. 23.

“The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions. We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation,” the company continued, referencing two Saudi-based airlines.

Delta noted that Saudi Arabia “remains an important market” for the company, adding it is “committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term.”

The weekend’s attacks on King Khalid resulted in the deaths of at least 13 people, including four Saudi citizens, one American, two Bangladeshi nationals, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Pakistani national , one Palestinian, one Sudanese national and one Syrian, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

The attacks, which the Houthis carried out on Saturday and Sunday, also injured at least 320 others, GACA reported. The aviation authority has suspended operations at the airport, located in the Saudi capital.

Airlines have canceled nearly 550 flights to and from King Khalid over the past 24 hours, according to data from FlightAware .

Before Delta announced the postponement of its Atlanta-to-Riyadh service launch, CEO Ed Bastian told CNBC on Monday that “safety” would dictate the company’s decision.

“Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week,” Bastian added.

The Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday advised U.S. pilots to “exercise caution” when flying in Saudi airspace due to risks associated with “ongoing military activities.” The notice is in effect until Dec. 10.

The State Department also advises Americans to “reconsider” travel to Saudi Arabia due to the risk of drone and missile attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group.

U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia need “special authorization” to use any airport in Saudi Arabia and cannot travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border due to safety risks, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh wrote Monday on social platform X.

articles.title: US military archbishop: Streamed execution threatens to ‘imitate the terrorists’
articles.summary: Archbishop Timothy Broglio, head of the Archdiocese for the Military Services, on Monday said he does not approve of the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, warning that it could “imitate the terrorists.” Broglio said in a statement released by the Archdiocese for the Military…
articles.body:
Archbishop Timothy Broglio, head of the Archdiocese for the Military Services, on Monday said he does not approve of the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, warning that it could “imitate the terrorists.”

Broglio said in a statement released by the Archdiocese for the Military Services that he sends his sympathy to the families and friends of Fort Hood shooting victims, noting that he presided over the funeral of one of those killed, Michael Grant Cahill.

He added that he sides with the Catholic Church’s opposition to capital punishment, “and Pope Francis made it even clearer.”

“Thirdly, do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries?” he continued. “The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?”

“Has the potential moral injury, which the members of the firing squad might experience, been considered?” Broglio inquired. “Will the exposure of a livestream to the young and impressionable during the 250th anniversary year of our independence be able to be repaired?”

He asked if there was any “value” in having the U.S. military thrown “in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world.”

“Does this decision reflect the dignity of the human person?” Broglio said before calling on service members to stop the livestream and urging Catholic members of the firing squad “to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the church.”

When asked by The Hill about Broglio’s remarks, the Pentagon referred to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s response to a CBS News social media post about the execution being livestreamed. His short response reads: “Correct.”

Hegseth on Thursday announced that the former U.S. Army major’s execution will be streamed and open to the public for viewing. The execution falls on Dec. 3, a Thursday, the same day of the week Hasan had planned his attack. It will also be held at Fort Hood, Hegseth said.

The announcement drew condemnation over its publicity. Democratic and Republican lawmakers urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision, with Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) warning that the stream could potentially fuel radicalization.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the choice , saying on Sunday that it is part of President Trump “restoring American values.” He dismissed concerns that it could fuel radicalization.

“I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” Mullin said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.” “I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies.”

articles.title: Oil prices spike after Houthi attacks on Saudi airports
articles.summary: Oil prices rose Monday, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia over the weekend. Brent Crude, the international benchmark, closed at nearly $106 per barrel as of late Monday afternoon, up roughly $1.20 from closing time Friday. The price of Brent Crude peaked at $107.33 earlier in the day. West…
articles.body:
Oil prices rose Monday, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia over the weekend.

Brent Crude, the international benchmark, closed at nearly $106 per barrel as of late Monday afternoon, up roughly $1.20 from closing time Friday. The price of Brent Crude peaked at $107.33 earlier in the day.

West Texas Intermediate Crude, the North American standard, reached $94.36 during Monday trading and closed at $93.16 per barrel .

The Houthis, a Yemen-based rebel group aligned with Iran, launched a string of attacks over the weekend on King Khalid International Airport and King Fahd International Airport , respectively located in Riyadh and Dammam, Saudi Arabia.

The pair of attacks on King Khalid killed at least 13 people and injured at least 320 others, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). GACA noted Sunday it was assessing the damage of the attack on King Fahd International Airport, which resulted in injuries.

President Trump said Saturday the U.S. “may” join Saudi Arabia in responding to the Houthis.

“We will make a decision. We move very quickly,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

Saudi forces, which the Obama administration and first Trump administration supplied with offensive weapons , have fought against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade.

The Iranian proxy group has continued to launch strikes into the kingdom during the U.S.-Iran war . The latter conflict, in its eighth month, has led to oil price spikes stemming from the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The shock to the energy industry has increased prices at the pump back home. As of Monday, a gallon of regular gas costs roughly $4.36 on average nationally, up about $1.28 from a year ago, according to data from AAA .

A gallon of diesel fuel also costs around $2.60 more on average than it did a year ago, AAA reported.

Trump on Friday announced a deal for Russia to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets, in an attempt to lower prices ahead of the midterms.

Under the deal, Russia will “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the marketplaces, before supplying another 500,000 tons next month, 1 million tons “immediately thereafter” and 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its diesel refineries, Trump wrote on Truth Social .

But analysts cautioned the deal may not lower prices, with GasBuddy’s Patrick De Haan saying Monday he was “skeptical” it will “deliver significant relief to the trucking industry and consumers who depend on diesel.”

articles.title: Trump Floats Potential Meeting With Kim Jong Un During Asia Trip
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during an upcoming trip to Asia, stoking speculation about renewed US outreach...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during an upcoming trip to Asia, stoking speculation about renewed US outreach to the reclusive regime.

"I may," Trump told reporters Monday when asked if he would meet with Kim during his trip. "That would be exciting."

Trump is slated to travel next month to the region, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

Trump has raised the prospect of another meeting with Kim in recent weeks, indicating he would like it to happen this year. The two leaders met thrice during the US president's first term, though those discussions failed to produce any diplomatic breakthroughs.

Still, Trump has repeatedly touted what he describes as warm relations between him and Kim. "I get along with him," Trump said on Monday.

Earlier this month, Trump also met with basketball star Dennis Rodman, who has traveled to North Korea multiple times and has had an unusual friendship with Kim.

North Korea has continued with a series of missile launches that have ratcheted up tensions in the region. On Monday, it fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said. It marked Pyongyang's fourth ballistic missile test in about a month.

Trump's overtures to North Korea come at a delicate moment in US-South Korea relations, with the two countries at odds over trade and security.

The US president has threatened to hit South Korea with new trade penalties if it does not follow through with an investment in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska, a $54 billion plan he has hailed as a centerpiece of Seoul's $350 billion investment commitment. The South Korean government has said it only agreed to the project if it proves economically viable.

In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back military exercises with South Korea, citing his frustration that Seoul declined to support US military operations against Iran and saying the drills sent an "inappropriate signal" to North Korea.

"When I found out it was drugs, I was very surprised." TSA Officer Isaiah Martinez Jr. then searched the carry-on and consulted with Stortz about the suspicious computer. articles.title: Alan Rick detalha estratégia para virada no 2º turno no Acre | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Republicanos abriu série de sabatinas da CBN Amazônia Rio Branco nesta terça (13). Em 30 minutos, senador detalhou propostas para infraestrutura, saúde e economia.
articles.summary: Candidato do Republicanos abriu série de sabatinas da CBN Amazônia Rio Branco nesta terça (13). Em 30 minutos, senador detalhou propostas para infraestrutura, saúde e economia.
articles.body:
Alan Rick (Republicanos) participou de entrevista na CBN Rio Branco nesta terça-feira (13) — Foto: Reprodução/CBN Rio Branco

O candidato ao governo do Acre Alan Rick ( Republicanos ) abriu, nesta terça-feira (13), a nova rodada de sabatinas da CBN Amazônia Rio Branco voltada ao 2º turno das eleições estaduais. A entrevista teve duração de 30 minutos e foi conduzida pelas jornalistas Rita Pontes e Bruna Rosa.

Após contabilizar 141.859 votos (32,27% dos votos válidos) na primeira etapa do pleito, disputando o 2º turno contra a candidata Mailza Assis (PP), que obteve 49%, o senador apresentou o detalhamento das suas propostas de governo e a estratégia política para buscar a virada eleitoral.

Logo no início da sabatina, ao ser questionado por ter vencido em apenas três dos 22 municípios acreanos no primeiro turno , Alan Rick afirmou que intensificará o diálogo direto com o eleitorado e com as lideranças locais.

"A força da máquina é esmagadora. O governo chega para os prefeitos e faz todo tipo de promessa [...] Nós não temos cargos para oferecer, nós não temos estrutura de secretarias para oferecer. O que nós temos para oferecer ao povo do Acre é um projeto de governo que traga de volta a esperança", destacou.

Sobre como pretende conduzir a gestão com as prefeituras em um eventual mandato, assegurou que adotará uma postura de cooperação institucional isenta de discriminação partidária.

O candidato destacou ainda a força da sua base aliada no Legislativo, citando a eleição de três deputados estaduais pelo Republicanos e dois pelo PSD, além do apoio da senadora eleita Mara Rocha (Republicanos) e do deputado federal reeleito Roberto Duarte, também do mesmo partido.

"A relação será a mais republicana possível: de apoio, de convênio. Acabou a eleição, todo mundo senta na mesa, todos os prefeitos, pra gente trabalhar pelo Acre [...] não deixarei de atender nenhum município", garantiu.

Alan Rick (Republicanos) participou de entrevista na CBN Rio Branco — Foto: Joás Linhares/CBN Rio Branco

Na pauta do agronegócio e desenvolvimento econômico, o candidato garantiu a manutenção dos incentivos fiscais em Áreas de Livre Comércio e ZPEs, além de propor a ampliação da utilização de áreas agriculturáveis de 20% para até 50%, dentro do que faculta o Código Florestal para estados com alta cobertura de preservação.

Em relação às finanças do estado, Alan Rick defendeu que é possível recuperar a capacidade de investimento do Acre sem a necessidade de aumentar impostos. Segundo o parlamentar, a contenção de gastos virá do combate a irregularidades e da revisão de contratos considerados superestimados.

"Nós não precisamos aumentar impostos. Se a gente trouxer o investimento, isso vai gerar arrecadação, vai trazer nova fonte de renda pro estado, pra podermos fazer os investimentos. O governo federal será um governo, se Deus quiser, parceiro nosso com Flávio Bolsonaro. Nós vamos ter um governo federal amigo do Acre, que vai nos ajudar a concluir a BR-364, fazer as revisões, nos ajudar com recurso para as nossas estradas vicinais e pro nosso programa de pavimentação dos ramais", comentou.

Alan Rick promete melhorias na saúde e na educação em entrevista na CBN Rio Branco nesta terça (13) — Foto: Reprodução/CBN Rio Branco

Na saúde, o plano apresentado prevê a regionalização do atendimento hospitalar no interior por meio da fixação de equipes com médicos especialistas. A medida, segundo Alan, busca resolver os problemas de deslocamento de pacientes e reduzir as filas no Pronto-Socorro de Rio Branco, combinada à proposta de construir um novo hospital no Segundo Distrito da capital.

"Vamos trazer para os hospitais do interior do estado a segurança para o paciente fazer o seu atendimento no próprio município, como com as equipes de médicos especialistas, o anestesista, o cirurgião-geral, o pediatra, ginecologista e obstetra, uma equipe com enfermeiros, com equipe de saúde qualificada, mantendo esse profissional no interior para que o atendimento seja realizado no município. Nós precisamos de verdade regionalizar a saúde, construir um novo pronto-socorro, um hospital metropolitano no Segundo Distrito de Rio Branco. O atual, infelizmente, não está dando conta", criticou.

Na educação, defendeu a valorização das carreiras docentes, a renovação dos contratos de professores provisórios, a expansão de escolas cívico-militares e a ampliação do programa de conectividade Wi-Fi Brasil em escolas rurais.

"A educação será valorizada, escolas com internet, ensino técnico profissionalizante no terceiro, no segundo turno, mais escolas cívico-militares, mais parcerias com os prefeitos também para a criação de novas creches. Um governo parceiro, um governo amigo que vai fazer a educação do Acre verdadeiramente qualificar e preparar os nossos jovens e adolescentes para o Enem, para o mercado de trabalho", prometeu.

Nas considerações finais da entrevista, Alan Rick convocou os eleitores para o segundo turno e reforçou sua confiança na mudança de cenário político no estado:

"A eleição está 0 a 0. Não acredite nessa história de que 'já ganhou' deles [...] O Acre vai mudar. O Acre terá um governador trabalhador que vai cuidar da educação, da saúde, da segurança, da geração de emprego", disse.

Kyiv’s allies, including those in President Trump’s circle, are rallying around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, pushing back against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and threats to cut off weapons and intelligence sharing to Ukraine.

articles.title: Scammers are stealing checks from the mail. Here’s how to protect yours
articles.summary: Check fraud doubled from 2021 to 2023 as postal inspectors recover over $1 billion in counterfeit checks yearly. Here's how to protect payments.
articles.body: You try to use your credit card to make a purchase and are told it has been declined. In a panic, you call your credit card company, which informs you that they never received your last payment. "That’s impossible," you exclaim, knowing you sent in the payment weeks ago. You go to check other recently paid bills to find out that several others, including your housing association fees and insurance payments, weren’t received. You head to your bank, only to find out that the checks have been "washed" — that is, fished out of the mail, ink lifted and re-made out to other people. This exact scam happened to one of my family members, and per the U.S. Postal Service, these scams are surging, with Postal Inspectors recovering "more than $1 billion in counterfeit checks and money orders every year." The U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has said that check fraud doubled from 2021 to 2023! 6 IN 10 IDENTITY CRIMES NOW BEGIN WITH A NEW ACCOUNT My family member thought she did everything right. She avoided online payments so she wouldn’t be subject to online payment scams. The checks were dropped off at the local post office in a box right outside the facility. But still, she ended up being scammed (which fortunately, with the help of her bank, she wasn’t liable for the clearly stolen funds). So, even if the mail isn’t safe, how can you protect yourself? First, use a special pen. Check washing uses a chemical process to remove the ink. Using a gel pen can make this process more difficult for criminals to do. Also, pressing hard when writing can make it more difficult to erase. However, this is not a foolproof plan either, as many authorities are noting that scammers are now using technology to scan the checks with your signature and reproduce fake copies using their computers. So, the pens can help as a deterrent, but aren’t 100% safe, either. Consider paying in person If you have the ability to do so, pay your bills in person. For example, pay your credit card at a local associated branch of the company. Pay your property taxes at the city’s offices. Of course, it’s less convenient, but a lot more secure. You can also consider paying online, but this opens you up to online scams, so make sure you do so safely, using best practices. If you choose to use the mail, drop it off inside the post office. Don’t use mailboxes. Yes, it’s less convenient, but even the boxes owned by the government are targeted by scammers, so physically go into the post office to drop off your mail. As a bonus tip, guard your mail at home. Get your mail frequently so that scammers can’t pull information from your mailbox. If you plan to travel, put a free hold on your mail delivery with the post office while you are away. Monitor your payment status regularly. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE Acting quickly can help to make sure you recover any misappropriated funds. Designate a day a week to be "bill day" and make sure all your bills have been paid, and the payments have gone through as expected. If any payment is taking too long to process, look into it immediately. Contact your financial institution to help you through this process. Be diligent, even when you are doing something as routine as mailing a check.

articles.title: Fake Facebook Marketplace listing uses your name
articles.summary: A fake Facebook Marketplace text scam uses your real name as the seller to trick you into replying, and Malwarebytes warns even one response helps.
articles.body: You get a text message from a number you don't recognize asking a pretty normal question: "Is this still available for purchase?" Attached to the text is an image that appears to show a Facebook Marketplace listing. Maybe you're confused because you don't remember selling anything. Then you look at the seller's name. It's yours. That small detail could be enough to make you respond with something like, "That's not me." And that reaction may be exactly what the person behind the message wants. Security researchers at Malwarebytes are warning about a personalized text scam that uses fabricated Facebook Marketplace listings with the recipient's name as the seller. The message can create an immediate fear that someone is impersonating you online. Here's how this scam pulls you in and what you should do if one of these texts lands on your phone. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET How the fake Facebook Marketplace listing works Malwarebytes analyzed an example sent through iMessage. The text asked whether an item was still available and included an image resembling a Facebook Marketplace listing. The clever part appears when you look at the supposed seller. The recipient's real name is there. However, Malwarebytes noticed something strange. The profile photo did not belong to the recipient. Researchers traced the picture to another Facebook user who happened to have the same name. That suggests the scammer may have started with a name and matching phone number. Those details could potentially come from breached data or another source. The attacker could then use the name to build a convincing fake Marketplace screenshot. Seeing your name creates an obvious question: "Is someone pretending to be me?" Before you know it, you're typing a reply. Why scammers want you to respond This technique is known as a conversation lure. Instead of immediately asking for a password or sending an obvious phishing link, the sender gives you a reason to start talking. In this case, the lure feels personal. Someone apparently put your name on a Marketplace listing. You may want to correct the buyer or find out what happened. You might also worry that someone has created a fake Facebook account in your name. The exact motive behind this particular campaign remains unclear because determining the next step would require engaging with the sender. Still, replying to suspicious texts carries its own risk. The Federal Trade Commission warns that even replying to an unexpected text can confirm that a scammer has reached a working telephone number. That could lead to more scam calls and texts. Your reply may tell scammers more than you realize Think about how harmless a response such as "wrong person" feels. You haven't shared a password or sent money. You haven't clicked a suspicious website. However, you've given the sender something useful: confirmation that someone is actively using the number and willing to respond. Malwarebytes reports that a live number can become more valuable to scammers and potentially be resold to others. The number could also be combined with additional information gathered from public profiles, breached databases or other sources. That can help set up another scam. You might later receive a fake delivery alert. Another message could pretend to come from your bank. A scammer might eventually try to steal a verification code, direct you to a malicious site or build a longer conversation designed to gain your trust. We recently looked at what a scammer can do with your name, phone number and address. Those details can become far more useful when criminals combine them with other personal information. How AI could make personalized scams easier to scale Creating individual Marketplace screenshots for thousands of people once would have required a lot of tedious work. AI and automation can change that equation. Malwarebytes says an attacker with a list containing names and phone numbers could potentially use an AI agent to help create personalized lures at scale. However, researchers have not established that AI created the specific example they examined. Still, automation makes this kind of personalization much easier to produce. That's an important shift in how we should judge suspicious messages. A text knowing your name provides little reassurance that the sender actually knows you. Personal information gets exposed through breaches, scraped from public sources and traded in criminal marketplaces. Once scammers connect a few pieces, they can make a random message feel surprisingly personal. Does this mean your Facebook account was hacked? No. Seeing your name on one of these fake Marketplace images does not, by itself, mean someone has accessed your Facebook account. The Marketplace screenshot may simply be fabricated. That's why I would resist the urge to reply to the sender asking what's going on. Instead, check Facebook yourself. What Apple says about suspicious iMessages Apple says this type of deceptive messaging uses social engineering, a tactic in which scammers rely on impersonation and manipulation to persuade people to share personal information. Criminals may pretend to represent a trusted company or organization while trying to obtain passwords, security codes or financial details. Apple also points to an important iMessage protection. By default, users cannot open links sent by an unknown iMessage sender until they add that person to their contacts or reply to the message. That gives you another reason to avoid responding to an unexpected text. Apple recommends treating suspicious, unexpected messages as potential scams and contacting the company directly through a trusted channel. The company also says users can filter unknown senders, report suspicious messages and block unwanted contacts through Messages. How to protect yourself from scam texts on iPhone Apple's Messages app includes tools to help filter unwanted texts, report suspicious messages and block senders. Since this Facebook Marketplace scam arrives through iMessage, here's how to use those protections on an iPhone. Turn on screening for unknown senders Messages from unknown senders will appear in a separate folder instead of your main conversation list. Apple says you won't receive notifications for these messages unless you've chosen to allow certain categories of unknown messages. SCAMMERS KNOW THE BEST TIME TO TEXT YOU Report a suspicious iMessage Apple says reporting an iMessage sends the sender's information and message content to Apple. The message is then permanently deleted from your iPhone. However, reporting does not automatically block the sender, so follow the blocking steps below. If you have already replied, the reporting option may no longer be available. For SMS, MMS or RCS messages that don't display a reporting option, Apple recommends contacting your wireless carrier directly. Block the scammer's number Blocking prevents messages from that number from reaching you. The sender won't receive a notification that you've blocked them. Check messages Apple has flagged as spam Important: These protections can reduce exposure to scam messages, but they cannot guarantee that every personalized phishing attempt will be detected. Don't reply to a suspicious Marketplace message simply because it contains your real name. How to stay safe from fake Facebook Marketplace texts A message like this is designed to make you react. Instead, give yourself a moment and investigate through channels you trust. 1) Don't reply to the text Even telling the sender they have the wrong person can confirm that somebody is actively using the number. The FTC recommends avoiding replies to unexpected messages from unknown numbers. 2) Don't use links or contact information in the message Don't click a link, call a number or scan a QR code supplied in the conversation. Never send the person a one-time security code or a screenshot containing security information. If you need to check Facebook, open the app yourself or type the address directly into your browser. 3) Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software can help protect you if a scammer eventually sends a malicious link or tries to get you to download malware. It can also warn you about some dangerous websites before they cause trouble. The best way to protect yourself from malicious links that install malware and potentially access your private information is to have antivirus software installed on all your devices. This protection can also alert you to phishing emails and ransomware scams, keeping your personal information and digital assets safe. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM 4) Check your Facebook account independently Open Facebook and review your Marketplace activity and messages. Look for anything you didn't post or send. You should also review your account security for unfamiliar logins, changed contact information or other activity you don't recognize. 5) Check with a known sender another way If a suspicious message appears to come from someone you actually know, contact that person through a different method. For example, call a number you already have saved rather than using contact information supplied in the suspicious message. 6) Report and block suspicious texts On an iPhone, follow the reporting and blocking steps above. Android users can use their messaging app's built-in spam reporting and blocking features. The FTC also recommends forwarding unwanted texts to 7726 (SPAM). These reports can help wireless providers identify and block similar messages. 7) Report a Facebook impersonator If you discover that someone really has created a Facebook profile pretending to be you, preserve the profile's URL and report it to Facebook. A fake screenshot alone does not prove that an impersonating Facebook profile actually exists. Check Facebook independently before assuming someone has created one. 8) Secure your Facebook account if something looks wrong If you discover an unfamiliar login, changed account information or other evidence of unauthorized access, start Facebook's account recovery process immediately. You should also review your password and enable two-factor authentication (2FA). Facebook currently places its two-factor authentication controls under Accounts Center > Password and security > Two-factor authentication. 9) Reduce the personal information scammers can find This scam shows why exposed personal information can be so useful to criminals. Your name and phone number may already appear on people-search sites or in data-broker databases. Removing that information won't erase data already exposed in a breach, but it can reduce what scammers can easily find and use to personalize future attacks. While no service can promise to remove all your data from the internet, a data removal service can monitor and automate the process of removing your information from hundreds of sites continuously over a longer period. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. What if you already replied? Don't assume a single response means your phone or Facebook account has been compromised. A reply alone does not give someone access to your Facebook account. What you should do next depends on how far the interaction went. Kurt's key takeaways What makes this scam so convincing is the personal detail. You see your own name on a Marketplace listing you never created, and, of course, you want to know what's going on. That's exactly why you should avoid replying to the stranger who sent it. Instead, open Facebook yourself and check your account. If you don't see the listing or any suspicious activity, report the text, block the sender and move on. If something looks wrong, secure your Facebook account right away. The bigger concern here is how easily scammers can use pieces of our personal information to make a random text feel legitimate. Your name and phone number may already be available through a data breach, data broker or another source. Seeing accurate information about yourself in an unexpected message should make you more cautious, not more trusting. Scammers keep finding new ways to use our personal information against us, so who should bear more responsibility for stopping these attacks before they reach our phones? articles.title: DOJ apologizes after campaign-style Trump ads air in violation of judge’s order
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) apologized late Monday for a controversial ad featuring President Trump that continued to run after a court sided with government watchdog groups in temporarily blocking the ads. Common Cause and a coalition of other groups, including a candidate for an Alabama state House seat, sued over the ads, arguing the…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) apologized late Monday for a controversial ad featuring President Trump that continued to run after a court sided with government watchdog groups in temporarily blocking the ads.

Common Cause and a coalition of other groups, including a candidate for an Alabama state House seat, sued over the ads, arguing the Trump administration broke the law in using federal funds for an ad that amounts to a campaign expenditure.

The plaintiffs won a temporary restraining order in the case late Sunday, but they complained to the court that the ad was not yet off the airwaves by Monday.

“The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs,” a Justice Department attorney wrote in an update to the court.

The attorney said some federal workers did not see the judge’s order until the holiday Monday, leading to a delay in canceling the already purchased ad time.

“Defendants understand that they are enjoined from using, disbursing, or transferring funds appropriated to the Department of Homeland Security to develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements; Defendants understand that they shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements,” the attorney wrote.

The Democratic National Committee has also sued over the ads, which show numerous images of the president overlaid with quotes from recent speeches demeaning communism while also crediting himself for the largest tax cuts in history.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, one of which features the song “Love Me” by artist JMSN, who said the song was used without his permission .

articles.title: Higher Rates Turbocharge Lending Income for Biggest US Banks
articles.summary: Three of the biggest US banks set a fresh record in the third quarter for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as inte...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Three of the biggest US banks set a fresh record in the third quarter for how much they earned from lending, with customers continuing to borrow even as interest rates increased.

JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citigroup Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co. on Tuesday reported a combined $56.5 billion of net interest income in the period, setting a new high-water mark for a fifth straight quarter. JPMorgan predicted that NII will be even higher in 2027.

That outlook represents a significant shift from earlier this year, when banks expected interest rates to drop and blockbuster trading hauls grabbed most of investors' attention. That overshadowed the more traditional business of earning money from loans and other interest-bearing assets.

Banks also see consumers and businesses maintaining their ability keep up with loan payments. All three companies reported fewer so-called non-accrual loans, those from which the firms stop recognizing interest income. Bank of America Corp. is set to reported third-quarter results on Wednesday.

Still, the lenders are remaining cautious amid an array of geopolitical uncertainties, including wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, stubborn inflation and elevated oil prices.

JPMorgan is "just making sure we're really scrubbing everything," Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. "There's capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms, we just need to be really, really on top of things to make sure that nothing slips through."

articles.title: Fort Hood massacre survivor weighs in on possible Hasan execution livestream
articles.summary: Fort Hood massacre survivor Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford shared his complicated feelings on the planned execution of convicted shooter Nidal Hasan potentially being livestreamed in December. Appearing on The Hill’s partner network NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight,” Lunsford stated he was “excited about the firing squad” planned for Hasan’s execution. “In terms of it being livestreamed, I…
articles.body:
Fort Hood massacre survivor Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford shared his complicated feelings on the planned execution of convicted shooter Nidal Hasan potentially being livestreamed in December.

Appearing on The Hill’s partner network NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight,” Lunsford stated he was “excited about the firing squad” planned for Hasan’s execution.

“In terms of it being livestreamed, I mean, for mature adults, if you want to watch it, watch it,” he said. “If you don’t, don’t. But I have an issue with kids viewing this. Kids and adolescents, this is not for their young minds.”

“The young minds are not in a position to process seeing a horrific act or the back end of being a murderer the way that Hasan was and what he did for him to pay for his crime. It’s not for everybody’s eyes. It’s not a thing where we’re going to have a tailgate,” Lunsford continued.

“That’s not what we stand for. So, I mean, that’s just my gut feeling on this whole situation,” he concluded.

Lunsford survived the shooting at Fort Hood where 13 members of the U.S. Army were killed and 32 were injured, most of whom were military personnel in what was the deadliest mass shooting ever on a U.S. military installation.

Hasan has remained on the U.S. military’s death row since he was sentenced to death in 2013.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced last week that Hasan’s execution would be streamed and open to the public for viewing and also be held at Fort Hood, which drew almost immediate criticism from both sides of the aisle.

Hegseth has said he wanted the “harshest lawful punishment” for Hasan; however, President Trump said on Saturday, he will “ make a decision ultimately ” about whether the execution will be shown live.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) criticized the possibility of the execution being livestreamed, saying she expected such a decision from “terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

Archbishop Timothy Broglio, head of the Archdiocese for the Military Services, also disapproved of the livestreamed execution, warning that it could “ imitate the terrorists .”

“The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose,” Broglio asked in a Monday statement .

articles.title: El-Sayed labels AI ‘existential threat’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) labeled AI an “existential threat” Tuesday, as he laid out a framework that aims to get the technology “under control.” El-Sayed, who is locked in a tight race with former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), called for a pause on frontier AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence. “Right…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) labeled AI an “existential threat” Tuesday, as he laid out a framework that aims to get the technology “under control.”

El-Sayed, who is locked in a tight race with former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), called for a pause on frontier AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence .

“Right now, the whims of a few tech billionaires are the only thing stopping AI from developing to the point that it poses an existential threat to humanity,” he said in a statement. “That is unacceptable.”

He pointed to a series of recent cybersecurity incidents involving AI agents and stark warnings from researchers about the technology’s potential consequences for humanity, arguing there needs to be a halt in development until sufficient guardrails are in place.

Under an earlier iteration of his AI platform, El-Sayed suggested all frontier AI companies should be chartered as public benefit corporations and divested from major tech companies, with the public holding a 50 percent stake in the firms and receiving dividends.

He also called for restrictions on the technology, barring it from denying medical care, independently firing weapons, conducting mass surveillance and making life-or-death decisions.

His latest AI framework seeks to bar recursive self-improvement, in which AI trains and improves itself, and require AI kill switches that could shut down the systems if needed.

El-Sayed also argued for the creation of a cabinet-level AI safety agency, mandatory reporting of security incidents and criminal penalties for executives who “recklessly break the rules.”

“Donald Trump, Mike Rogers, and their Big Tech billionaire donors can’t be trusted to keep either Michigan or humanity safe from the existential dangers of unrestrained AI,” he added Tuesday.

Trump has taken a more hands-off approach to AI regulation, seeking to allow the companies to police themselves amid concerns that stricter limits could cause the U.S. to fall behind China.

But Rogers has sought some distance from the president on the issue, calling for a slowdown in AI development “to allow the government and its partners to catch up and put stricter protocols and guardrails in place.”

articles.title: Thousands of bottles of acetaminophen sold on Amazon recalled
articles.summary: Consumers reported finding discolored tablets, according to the recall notices.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Thousands of bottles of acetaminophen sold on Amazon have been recalled over reports of discolored tablets, according to a recall notice from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

The recalls, voluntarily issued last month but only recently included in the FDA’s enforcement report, impact nearly 113,000 bottles of 500-milligram Extra Strength Acetaminophen caplets available through Amazon.

There are three separate alerts on the FDA’s site for the following products:

14,640 200-count bottles with lot number ACD125040A and an expiration date of 09/30/2027

90,456 500-count bottles with multiple lot numbers and expiration dates: ACD124036A and ACD124030A, 09/30/2027 ACD124042A, 10/31/2027 ACD124048B, 11/30/2027 ACD125010A, 02/29/2028

7,836 1,000-count bottles with lot number ACD124048A and expiration date 11/30/2027

According to the alerts, customers reported discolored pills, prompting the recall.

“Amazon is voluntarily recalling specific lots of Amazon Basic Care Extra Strength Pain Relief acetaminophen 500mg caplets due to reports of tablet discoloration in the affected lots,” a spokesperson told Nexstar. “This is a voluntary recall initiated in coordination with the manufacturer, Aurohealth, and the FDA.”

If you have an impacted bottle, you likely have already been contacted. There have been no reported adverse impacts related to the acetaminophen included in the recall.

Acetaminophen is considered an analgesic and antipyretic, meaning it can relieve pain and reduce fevers, MedlinePlus explains , meaning it not only alters how your body senses pain but also helps to cool it.

Last year, Aurobindo issued a similar recall for 325-milligram Acetaminophen Tablets sold on Amazon due to discoloration of the pills. A notice from Aurobindo said some consumers had noticed a “brown surface on tablets.”

In 2022, the company recalled more than 160,000 bottles of acetaminophen — about 137,300 units of Walgreens brand acetaminophen and roughly 25,660 units of Kroger brand arthritis pain acetaminophen — due to issues with child-resistant packaging.

articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a coalition of seven states asked a federal court on Tuesday to punish Martin Shkreli for “flagrantly and repeatedly” violating a lifetime ban from being involved in the pharmaceutical industry.

In a court filing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the FTC said Shkreli has traded in at least 60 pharmaceutical stocks since being released from prison in 2022. He’s also been broadcasting his opinions about the business and management of the companies through livestreaming and posting on numerous social media platforms.

The coalition asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt and institute penalties, including forcing him to forfeit all trading profits and sell all his pharmaceutical stock.

The filing asked the court to demand Shkreli pay a fine equal to his profits from trading on pharma stocks and face consequences for any future violations, “including financial penalties and potential incarceration.”

“A court-ordered lifetime ban isn’t a suggestion,” New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) said in a statement. “Martin Shkreli has been livestreaming his pharmaceutical company trades for the world to see, in violation of the law. Shkreli’s market manipulation and monopolistic tactics put investors and the public at risk, and we’re going back to court to put a stop to his latest illegal behavior.”

Shkreli became known as “pharma bro” in 2015 for unapologetically raising the price of an anti-parasitic drug called Daraprim by 5,000 percent. Shkreli notoriously told Congress he should have increased the price more and maintained he did nothing wrong.

He was separately convicted of three counts of fraud in 2017 and sentenced to seven years in prison. He was released in 2022.

Prior to his release, a federal court banned him from ever working in the drug industry again, saying he illegally tried to prevent generic competition to Daraprim.

Despite the court’s order, the FTC in the filing said Shkreli has openly traded pharmaceutical stocks and publicly discussed the industry at length, encouraging his social media followers to invest based on his recommendations.

This isn’t the first time Shkreli has been accused of flouting the lifetime ban. The FTC in 2023 asked the court to hold Shkreli in contempt for failing to pay a $65 million fine and for not cooperating with an investigation into his role in the formation of a software company called Druglike.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
articles.body:
The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.

Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said.

Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet.

Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach.

Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense.

Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating.

That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts.

When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway.

“In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.”

Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying.

“We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said.

In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools.

To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do.

What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation.

“We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained.

The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.

She said 70% of Pluto’s sales pipeline now comes from inbound interest, although she didn’t break down how much of that comes directly through Plutonium.

Pluto said it plans to invest the new capital in developing its product, expanding its security research efforts, and growing its presence in the U.S. It has 40 employees in the U.S. and Israel.
