articles.title: OPEC cuts oil demand projections for remainder of 2026
articles.summary: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) lowered its forecast of global oil demand growth for this year, amid persistent risks to shipping from Iran and its proxy groups. The group projected Tuesday that oil demand for this year will grow by roughly 200,000 barrels per day relative to 2025, down from OPEC’s forecast…
articles.body:
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) lowered its forecast of global oil demand growth for this year, amid persistent risks to shipping from Iran and its proxy groups.

The group projected Tuesday that oil demand for this year will grow by roughly 200,000 barrels per day relative to 2025, down from OPEC’s forecast in September of about 400,000 barrels per day.

OPEC’s forecast of 2026 oil demand also fell last month from roughly 600,000 barrels per day in August , as the Iran war and its spillover impacts on the energy industry persist.

“Heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, disruptions to regional crude flows, and strong demand for prompt barrels pushed front-month prices higher relative to forward prices,” OPEC’s monthly report stated.

The group of oil-rich nations has 11 members, including Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.

Throughout the Iran conflict , which the U.S. and Israel launched in late February, the Iranian military has restricted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz — through which nearly 34 percent of the world’s crude oil passed last year, according to the International Energy Agency .

While President Trump said Monday the U.S. is in “control” of the strait amid American forces’ blockade of Iranian ports, data from July and August show that shipping activity in the waterway was “highly restricted,” according to the World Trade Organization (WTO).

“Only isolated shipments were visible around the end of July, early August, and again in mid-August. These sporadic movements were insufficient to generate a sustained increase in the moving average, which remained close to zero through most of August,” the WTO noted last month.

The Iran-backed Houthis have also recently targeted ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman and launched strikes over the weekend at two airports in Saudi Arabia.

Those attacks sparked a rise in oil prices on Monday, with Brent crude , the international benchmark, peaking at $107.33 per barrel.

But the price of Brent crude is down slightly on Tuesday, with the commodity trading at less than $106 per barrel as of the mid-afternoon. West Texas Intermediate crude, the North American benchmark, is up roughly 40 cents from closing time Monday.

Challenges that the oil industry is facing will not slow demand for petroleum next year, OPEC projected.

The organization raised its forecast for global oil demand in 2027 to about 2.6 million barrels per day, up from its September projection of roughly 2.4 million barrels per day.

articles.title: Top Army general reassures defense industry after Driscoll, George exits
articles.summary: The Army’s acting chief of staff, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, assured the defense industry on Tuesday that the military’s largest branch is not walking away from modernization after losing top brass earlier this year, but is in fact “sprinting towards it.” “And to our industry partners in this room, we need you to hear this: the…
articles.body:
The Army’s acting chief of staff, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, assured the defense industry on Tuesday that the military’s largest branch is not walking away from modernization after losing top brass earlier this year, but is in fact “sprinting towards it.”

“And to our industry partners in this room, we need you to hear this: the secretary and I are not walking away from modernization. This is clearly captured in the Army Azimuth, where I lay forth the requirements to outpace our adversaries, and I hope that after yesterday’s remarks from Acting Army Secretary [Adam] Telle, you can see that our Army values American ingenuity to help us with this,” LaNeve said during the Dwight D. Eisenhower luncheon at a military conference in Washington, D.C.

“No, the Army’s not turning its back on modernization. In fact, quite the opposite. We are sprinting towards it,” LaNeve, who was picked for the role after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staf f Gen. Randy George, said at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA).

LaNeve, also the Army’s vice chief of staff, made the remarks as the new Army leadership looks to refine priorities for modernization efforts advocated by George and former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned in late August after months of clashes with Hegseth.

“Our investments must strengthen the Army as a collective warfighting system rather than attempt to make every platform technologically superior or equip every formation with every capability. We will concentrate resources on the capabilities essential to Convergence, Strike, Close Battle and Endurance,” the branch said in the “How the Army Fights,” a 46-page framework , signed by LaNeve, which was published last week.

The Army Transformation Initiative, which was rolled out last April, encouraged technological experimentation across the force, cut bureaucracy and redirected resources to top-priority operational capabilities.

“The Army cannot and should not modernize everything at once,” the branch said in the framework. “The answer is focused modernization.”

Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, said on Monday that the Army has to move at the “speed of business” and not the speed of government as the Trump administration continues to rearrange how the branch operates and innovates.

“We were taking too long to find and fund good ideas. That’s because we based who we did business with not on how well they could deliver equipment or innovation to our soldiers, but based on whether their bureaucracy was big enough to interface with our big bureaucracy,” Telle said during his Monday appearance at AUSA. “Agile, hungry companies with brilliant ideas were starved while we forced them to wait.”

Army leaders have said the recent push to spur investment and innovation is necessary to shake up the status quo, but it is now up to leadership to make “threat-informed investments,” LaNeve said on Tuesday.

The Army will decide which technologies need funding and where they will be implemented as the service branch’s resources are not “endless,” LaNeve said.

“This means making thoughtful decisions over where investments are made. And when I think of Army capabilities, I bend them into three categories, and I’ve talked to you a lot about this on the floor: legacy, enduring, and modern,” the acting Army chief of staff said. “We’re going to divest legacy equipment with the intention to unburden our units as fast as we can from the old and failing equipment that distracts us from meaningful training.”

“We will purposely invest in our enduring capabilities that halve the bridge time for us to get the modern equipment into the force,” he said on Tuesday. “But we will also make intentional investments for modern capabilities that can be scaled and directly contribute to how the Army fights within the joint force.”

articles.title: Trump administration seeks to reconsider offshore wind farm’s approval
articles.summary: The Trump administration is asking a federal court to reassess a prior approval of a nearly-completed offshore wind farm, an escalation of the administration’s attack on wind energy that’s raising questions about an infrastructure deal with Democrats. On Friday, the Trump administration asked Judge Roy Lamberth to allow it to reassess whether its past approval…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is asking a federal court to reassess a prior approval of a nearly-completed offshore wind farm, an escalation of the administration’s attack on wind energy that’s raising questions about an infrastructure deal with Democrats .

On Friday, the Trump administration asked Judge Roy Lamberth to allow it to reassess whether its past approval of the Revolution Wind Project was warranted.

It cited the project’s “potential moderate to major adverse impacts to other uses” of the area off the nation’s coast.

The move is one of a series of attacks the administration has instituted on renewable power and especially wind energy, a particular subject of President Trump’s scorn.

However, this latest action comes as the administration is working on a deal with Democrats that seeks to expedite the buildout of energy and infrastructure projects across the board.

Last month, Senate Democrats and Republicans said they had reached a deal on legislation that seeks to speed the buildout of various types of energy including renewables and fossil fuels by curtailing environmental laws and other provisions.

As the package was being negotiated, the Trump administration’s treatment of renewables was a key point of contention.

When the deal was announced, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said that one outstanding issue was “the question of returning to regular order for wind and solar projects in the Trump administration.”

“That is unresolved, but we have had what I would consider to be a very reasonable opening proposal from the Trump administration,” he said at the time.

It’s unclear whether the latest maneuver will impact efforts to get the legislation across the finish line. Lawmakers are expected to take up the bill in the lame duck session later this year.

White House official Jarrod Agen said in a post on the social platform X that the administration still supports the bipartisan deal.

“This is an old lawsuit brought by the local community—who had serious concerns about this project—against the Biden Administration!” wrote Agen, the executive director of the National Energy Dominance Council.

“The White House maintains support for PERMITTING REFORM! We look forward to the Senate voting on this historic legislation,” he added.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department said the filing is not a change in its position.

“The Department of the Interior is complying with a briefing schedule, not announcing a policy change. Our position has remained consistent throughout this administration and this filing should not be misconstrued as a shift in the Department’s approach to offshore wind,” said a spokesperson, who did not provide their name, in an email.

Revolution Wind is located off the coast of Rhode Island and is expected to supply enough power for 350,000 homes in Rhode Island and Connecticut.

The Trump administration’s filing comes in a case after various individuals and organizations challenged the approval of the project in 2024.

articles.title: Iran war costing US households average of $2K each: Moody’s
articles.summary: The war in Iran has cost the average American household $2,000 so far, according to estimates shared Monday by Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. “Consider that the war’s costs taken together have absorbed about half the average American household’s income gain over the past eight months,” Zandi wrote on X. “No wonder the…
articles.body:
The war in Iran has cost the average American household $2,000 so far, according to estimates shared Monday by Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics.

“Consider that the war’s costs taken together have absorbed about half the average American household’s income gain over the past eight months,” Zandi wrote on X . “No wonder the war is so unpopular.”

The conflict, which started in late February, has cost U.S. consumers $265 billion nationwide, Moody’s estimates show.

Zandi wrote that energy prices are the most significant contributor to rising costs. A gallon of gasoline costs $4.34, up from $2.98 a gallon before the conflict started, CNN reported . The average cost of diesel is close to $5.8 per gallon, up from $3.1 a year ago, according to AAA .

“Altogether, that comes to close to $1,100 per household, paid at the pump and in the higher cost of everything that moves by truck or plane,” Zandi wrote.

Zandi’s calculations also take into account the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates. Fixed mortgage rates rose from below 6% before the war to about 7.5% now.

“By our reckoning, the higher rates have cost the economy about $540 per household,” he wrote.

The cost of military operations adds up to about $360 per household, according to Zandi’s calculations. In early May, during an appearance in front of the House Appropriations Committee, the Pentagon’s acting chief financial officer, Jules Hurst III, told lawmakers the cost of the conflict was nearing $29 billion.

In late June, the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank, estimated the cost of the operations to be $38.6 billion, The Hill reported . The Center for Strategic and International Studies, in its late-June report , placed the cost at around $40 billion.

In June, the White House requested $87 billion in supplemental funding to help cover the cost of some stockpile replacements and troop deployments in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) theater, The Hill reported . The bill will likely need Democratic votes to pass in the Senate.
